History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
40-year-old woman with 3-week history of progressive left-sided hearing reduction and constant left facial numbness; clinician suspects Bell’s palsy but requests same-day in-person neurological/otoscopic examination.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Reduced hearing in left ear and numbness along left jaw/ear region.  
• Onset/duration: Gradual onset ≈3 weeks ago; symptoms persist and have slightly worsened.  
• Laterality: Exclusively left-sided.  
• Associated symptoms: Intermittent left-sided tinnitus; occasional dizziness coinciding with ringing.  
• Pertinent negatives: No limb weakness, dysphagia, dysarthria, visual change, ear discharge, ear pain, pruritus, fever, or recent trauma.  
• Symptom modifiers: None reported.

Past Medical History:
• Nasal polyps – intermittent flares treated with intranasal spray; no recent complications.  
• Remote episode diagnosed as “labyrinthitis” (details not provided).  
• No chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• Intranasal spray for nasal polyps – dose/route/frequency not documented.  
• Rennie (antacid) as needed – dose/route/frequency not documented.

Allergies:
• Latex – reaction not specified.

Social History:
• Occupation: Professional jockey (horse racing).  
• Lives with partner; no pets.  
• Tobacco, alcohol, recreational substances: not discussed.

Family History:
• Brother with neurofibromatosis (type unspecified).  
• Otherwise non-contributory per patient.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded (video visit).  
• General / HEENT / Neuro: Not performed – requires in-person assessment.

Investigations:
• None to date. Planned: Same-day face-to-face visit for full neurological examination and otoscopy.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Unilateral (left) auditory deficit with facial numbness; Bell’s palsy considered but other retrocochlear pathology (e.g., vestibular schwannoma) must be excluded.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Vestibular schwannoma – supports: unilateral hearing loss, tinnitus, dizziness, facial sensory change, family history of NF; opposes: short 3-week timeline.  
2. Idiopathic facial-nerve neuritis (Bell’s palsy) – supports: unilateral facial symptoms, clinician impression; opposes: sensory rather than motor deficit, concurrent hearing loss.  
3. Ramsay Hunt syndrome – supports: unilateral otologic/neural symptoms; opposes: no pain or vesicular rash.

Issue 1: Left-sided auditory loss & facial numbness  
• Assessment: Etiology undifferentiated; needs cranial-nerve exam and otoscopy to confirm/exclude Bell’s palsy vs retrocochlear lesion.  
• Plan:  
  – Same-day in-person GP clinic appointment for full neurological and otoscopic assessment (book via support team).  
  – If facial nerve weakness confirmed ⇒ initiate Bell’s palsy pathway (e.g., prednisolone ± eye protection) – to be decided after exam.  
  – If findings suggest sensorineural loss or other cranial nerve involvement ⇒ arrange urgent audiometry and MRI internal auditory canals/CPA; consider ENT referral.  
  – Safety-net: advise patient to attend emergency care if sudden worsening, new weakness, severe vertigo, headache, or visual changes.  

Issue 2: Intermittent dizziness  
• Assessment: Likely secondary to primary ear/nerve pathology.  
• Plan: Address as part of above evaluation; consider vestibular assessment if persists.

Issue 3: Nasal polyps (stable)  
• Assessment: Currently asymptomatic; uses PRN intranasal spray.  
• Plan: Continue current regimen PRN; no additional action today.

General plan items:  
• Document latex allergy prominently in chart.  
• Medication reconciliation at next visit.  
• Follow-up: Results and further management plan to be communicated after today’s examination; routine clinic follow-up within 1 week or sooner if imaging ordered.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: No vitals or physical examination documented; smoking/alcohol history not obtained; reaction details for latex allergy not specified.  
• Transcript vs DDx conflicts: None noted (clinician’s provisional Bell’s palsy aligns with DDx list).  
• Transcript quality: Clear; minor conversational overlaps; no inaudible portions affecting clinical content.
